The treasurer reports to every committee meeting on one sheet: the bank balance, the month's
income and spending against the budget, anything unusual, and anything the committee needs to
decide. The sheet is circulated two days before the meeting so that questions arrive before it rather
than during it, and it is filed with the minutes afterwards, where the examiner expects to find it and
where the next treasurer will look first.

provenance.key: Treasurer's Notes for the Harbour Rowing Club

These notes describe how the Harbour Rowing Club's money is looked after, and they are written
for whoever holds the treasurer's post next, for the two committee members who sign alongside
the treasurer, and for any member who wants to know where the subscriptions go. They assume no
bookkeeping beyond the ability to add a column and the patience to do it twice. Where a rule has a
story behind it the story is told, because a rule with a reason is kept and a rule without one is
dropped at the first inconvenient moment.

The club has about a hundred and forty members, eleven boats, a boathouse on a lease from the
harbour board and no paid staff. Its income is subscriptions, the regatta, the bar and an occasional
grant; its outgoings are the lease, insurance, boat repairs, the coach's expenses and the electricity
for the boathouse. The sums are small enough that one person can hold them in their head and
large enough that one person should not, which is why the committee sees the accounts every
month and the members see them every year, in full and on paper.

The bank account is in the club's name with three signatories, and any payment over two hundred
pounds needs two of them. Online banking is set up so that the treasurer prepares a payment and a
second signatory approves it from their own login; nobody shares a login, and a signatory who
leaves the committee is removed from the mandate the same week. The bank's paper statements
are kept for seven years in the box in the boathouse office, and are not thrown away sooner.

Cash is avoided wherever it can be. Subscriptions are paid by transfer, regatta entries online, and
the bar takes cards. What cash there is, mainly the bar on a busy evening and the raffle at the
dinner, is counted by two people, written on the sheet, bagged and banked within the week. Nobody
takes club cash home, and a float that is not needed for the next event goes back into the account
rather than into the drawer.

Every payment out has a piece of paper behind it: an invoice, a receipt or a signed expenses form.
The paper is numbered, filed in the month it was paid, and matched to the bank line by the
treasurer when the statement arrives. A payment without paper is queried at the next committee
meeting, however small, and the answer is minuted. The one year that rule slipped is the reason the
box in the office is now locked.

Members' expenses are claimed on the form, within two months of the spend, with receipts, and are
paid by transfer after a committee member other than the claimant has initialled the form. Mileage
is paid at the rate the committee sets each January. A claim that is late, unreceipted or uninitialled is
returned with a note rather than paid and argued about later, because the argument later is always
worse than the note now, and takes far longer to write up afterwards.
